source: Enderton, Elements of Set Theory.pdf; rewritten seed rule
name: Extensionality axiom
statement: Sets with exactly the same members are equal.
conditions: For all x, x is in A iff x is in B.
typical_uses: Prove equality of sets by elementwise membership.
repair_templates: Prove both A subset B and B subset A.

source: Enderton, Elements of Set Theory.pdf; rewritten seed rule
name: Union and intersection by membership
statement: The union of a family contains exactly elements belonging to at least one member; the intersection contains exactly elements belonging to every member.
conditions: A is a set of sets.
conclusion: Membership in union and intersection is characterized by existential and universal quantifiers.
repair_templates: Write the membership quantifiers explicitly before manipulating the sets.

source: Enderton, Elements of Set Theory.pdf; rewritten seed rule
name: Kuratowski ordered pair
statement: The ordered pair <x,y> is defined as {{x},{x,y}} and uniquely determines x and y.
typical_uses: Encode relations and functions as sets.
bridge_lemmas: Singleton and pair axioms construct the encoding.
repair_templates: Apply the ordered-pair uniqueness theorem before comparing coordinates.

source: Enderton, Elements of Set Theory.pdf; rewritten seed rule
name: Inverse function criterion
statement: The inverse relation of a function is a function exactly when the original function is one-to-one; for a bijection it is a two-sided inverse.
conclusion: F inverse is functional iff F is injective, and bijectivity gives inverse maps both ways.
common_misuses: Calling an inverse relation a function without injectivity.
repair_templates: Prove injectivity before defining F^{-1} as a function.

source: Enderton, Elements of Set Theory.pdf; rewritten seed rule
name: Equivalence classes partition
statement: An equivalence relation on A has equivalence classes that are nonempty, pairwise disjoint, and cover A; two classes are equal iff their representatives are equivalent.
conditions: R is reflexive, symmetric, and transitive on A.
conclusion: The classes form a partition of A.
typical_uses: Construct quotient sets and well-defined induced maps.
common_misuses: Assuming distinct representatives yield distinct classes.
bridge_lemmas: If classes intersect, transitivity makes them equal.
repair_templates: Check representative independence using the class equality criterion.

source: Enderton, Elements of Set Theory.pdf; rewritten seed rule
name: Induction on natural numbers
statement: If a property holds for 0 and its truth at n implies truth at n plus 1, then it holds for every natural number.
conditions: The property is defined on omega.
conclusion: The property holds for all natural numbers.
typical_uses: Prove arithmetic identities and recursively defined facts.
common_misuses: Skipping the base case or using an invalid successor step.
bridge_lemmas: The natural numbers are the smallest inductive set.
repair_templates: State base and induction hypotheses separately.

source: Enderton, Elements of Set Theory.pdf; rewritten seed rule
name: Recursion theorem on omega
statement: Given an initial value and a successor rule on a set A, there is a unique function on omega satisfying the recursion equations.
conditions: A is a set, a is in A, and F:A->A.
conclusion: There is a unique h with h(0)=a and h(n+1)=F(h(n)).
typical_uses: Define addition, multiplication, powers, and sequences.
common_misuses: Using a rule that does not map A into A.
repair_templates: Specify codomain closure and initial value.

source: Enderton, Elements of Set Theory.pdf; rewritten seed rule
name: Uniqueness of Peano system
statement: Every Peano system is isomorphic to the constructed natural-number system (omega, successor, zero).
conclusion: There is a unique isomorphism preserving zero and successor.
typical_uses: Transfer induction and arithmetic between models.
common_misuses: Assuming equality rather than isomorphism of presentations.
repair_templates: Build both maps by recursion and prove they are inverse.

source: Enderton, Elements of Set Theory.pdf; rewritten seed rule
name: Cantor-Schroeder-Bernstein theorem
statement: If A injects into B and B injects into A, then there is a bijection between A and B.
conditions: There are injections A->B and B->A.
typical_uses: Prove cardinal equalities without constructing a direct bijection.
common_misuses: Using arbitrary functions instead of injections.
bridge_lemmas: Iterate the two injections to form invariant pieces.

source: Enderton, Elements of Set Theory.pdf; rewritten seed rule
name: Countable union of countable sets
statement: A countable union of countable sets is countable, assuming a choice function for the enumerations when needed.
conditions: The index set is countable and every member set is finite or countable.
conclusion: The union is finite or countable.
typical_uses: Control cardinalities of sequences and rational approximations.
common_misuses: Ignoring the choice needed to select enumerations.
bridge_lemmas: Encode pairs of natural numbers by a single natural number.
repair_templates: Specify enumerations or invoke countable choice.

source: Enderton, Elements of Set Theory.pdf; rewritten seed rule
name: Well-ordering theorem
statement: Every set can be well ordered, equivalently to the axiom of choice in ZF.
conditions: The axiom of choice is assumed for the equivalence direction.
conclusion: Every nonempty subset has a least element under some ordering.
typical_uses: Apply transfinite recursion and cardinal comparison.
common_misuses: Assuming the usual order on arbitrary sets is a well-order.
bridge_lemmas: Choice, Zorn, and well-ordering are equivalent principles.
repair_templates: State explicitly where choice is invoked.

source: Enderton, Elements of Set Theory.pdf; rewritten seed rule
name: Ordinal as transitive well-ordered set
statement: An ordinal is a transitive set well ordered by membership; each element of an ordinal is a smaller ordinal.
conditions: alpha is a transitive set and membership well orders alpha.
conclusion: Ordinals represent order types of well-ordered sets.
common_misuses: Treating arbitrary well-ordered sets as ordinals without an isomorphism.
bridge_lemmas: The empty set is the least ordinal and successors are alpha union {alpha}.

source: Enderton, Elements of Set Theory.pdf; rewritten seed rule
name: Transfinite induction
statement: If a property holds at alpha whenever it holds for every beta in alpha, then it holds for every ordinal in the target ordinal.
conditions: The property is defined on an ordinal or all ordinals under consideration.
conclusion: The property holds throughout the ordinal domain.
typical_uses: Prove ordinal recursion and rank facts.
common_misuses: Using only successor induction and missing limit ordinals.
bridge_lemmas: If the counterexample set is nonempty, its least element yields a contradiction.
repair_templates: Include the limit case through the full predecessor hypothesis.

source: Enderton, Elements of Set Theory.pdf; rewritten seed rule
name: Transfinite recursion
statement: A rule assigning a value from the previously defined restriction determines a unique function along any well-ordered domain, subject to set-existence hypotheses.
conditions: The domain is well ordered and the recursion rule is functional on earlier stages.
conclusion: There is a unique recursively defined function on the domain.
typical_uses: Define ordinal operations and hierarchy constructions.
common_misuses: Defining the value using the current or future value.
repair_templates: Rewrite the rule using only the initial segment before alpha.

source: Enderton, Elements of Set Theory.pdf; rewritten seed rule
name: Well-founded minimal-element principle
statement: A relation is well founded when every nonempty subset has a minimal element; equivalently, induction over the relation is valid.
conditions: R is a relation on A.
conclusion: Every nonempty R-subset has an R-minimal element and well-founded induction is sound.
common_misuses: Confusing minimal with least or assuming totality.
repair_templates: Choose a minimal counterexample and apply the induction hypothesis to its predecessors.
